text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London rallied sharply to a 20 month peak lifting benchmark July by almost 20 per cent at one stage, on frenzied buying spearheaded by roasters. Players apparently had the feeling that the robusta market was undervalued relative to New York, especially if robusta output is going to be cyclically down in 1997/98 and there were rumours of defaults. Moreover, switching of blends to incorporate more robustas could tighten supplies as well. May added $373 per tonne to close at $2,535 per tonne, while July closed $342 higher at $2,600 per tonne.

With the sharp rise in London arabica futures in New York had no difficulties to push through 300 cents/lb. July closed 19.25 cents/lb higher at 314.80 cents/lb, while September added 17.10 cents/lb to close at 273.80 cents/lb. Never before has the market seen such a rise in prices without a frost in Brazil. This week alone, the July contract has gained a staggering 57.95 cents/lb or more than 22 per cent.

The start of Brazil's winter is likely to keep the market well underpinned over the next two months. However, what will happen thereafter remains an open question and players should look for warning signals that the rally is over. Past experience shows that such dramatic rises end just as dramatically without warning.
UNITED STATES - Certified coffee stocks fell by 554 bags on May 28 to 49,258 bags compared to 49,712 bags on May 27. There were no bags pending grading.

UNITED STATES - The United States imported 1.961 million bags of coffee in February 1997, nearly 11 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1997 up to 3.681 million bags, slightly less than the 3.710 million bags imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 reached 19.4 million bags, up from 17.1 million bags imported the previous year. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/February 1997 were Guatemala (415,600 vs 359,500 bags), Mexico (0.907 vs 1.221 million bags), Brazil (350,900 vs 133,900 bags), Colombia (511,200 vs 463,700 bags) and Vietnam (461,200 vs 447,600 bags). The country exported 348,900 bags of coffee in January/February 1997, 32 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1996. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose to 2.1 million bags, up from 1.8 million bags exported in 1995.

MEXICO - It was rumored that the Mexican government plans to allow roasters to import 150,000 bags of arabica coffee. It was argued that exports have been so high this season, that a shortage has developed on the domestic market. Total exports in October/April 1996/97 reached 3.71 million bags, up from 3.47 million bags exported the same period in 1995/96. Total exports in crop year 1995/96 (October/September) soared to 4.6 million bags, up from 3.3 million bags exported in 1994/95.

POLAND - Poland imported 113,900 bags of coffee in December 1996, nearly 4 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports in calendar year 1996 up to 1.624 million bags which compares to 1.536 million bags imported the previous year and 1.442 million bags imported in 1994. Main suppliers of green coffee in 1996 were Ivory Coast (223,000 vs 211,200 bags), Colombia (121,000 vs 62,400 bags), Peru (122,500 vs 151,800 bags), India (185,900 vs 130,600 bags), Indonesia (386,100 vs 210,600 bags) and Vietnam (163,300 vs 263,100 bags). The country exported 88,200 bags of coffee in 1996 compared to 42,300 bags exported the previous year.
